An urban heat island refers to a metropolitan area that is significantly warmer than its surrounding rural areas due to human activities. Today we will examine how archaeologists use obsidian hydration dating to determine the age of ancient stone tools and artifacts. Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass that prehistoric humans widely used to manufacture sharp cutting tools, arrowheads, and blades. When an obsidian artifact is freshly chipped or manufactured, its newly exposed surface immediately begins absorbing microscopic moisture from the surrounding environment. Over hundreds or thousands of years, this absorbed water forms a distinct hydration layer beneath the surface of the glass. Because this hydration layer grows at a predictable, measurable rate over time, scientists can measure its thickness using specialized optical microscopes. By calculating the thickness of the hydration rind, archaeologists can estimate the exact time when the artifact was originally shaped by human hands. However, this dating method requires careful calibration because hydration rates vary significantly depending on local soil temperature and regional climate conditions.

Listen to part of a lecture in a marine biology class.
Today we explore the remarkable physiological adaptations that allow marine mammals, such as Weddell seals, to perform prolonged deep-diving maneuvers without oxygen. When diving deep underwater, these mammals face two major physiological challenges: extreme hydrostatic pressure and severe oxygen depletion. To survive these conditions, marine mammals exhibit a specialized reflex called the mammalian dive response. Upon submergence, their heart rate drops dramatically, sometimes to just a tenth of its normal resting rate, and peripheral blood vessels constrict sharply. This selective vasoconstriction redirects oxygen-rich blood away from non-essential muscles and organs, reserving the limited oxygen supply exclusively for the brain and heart. Furthermore, their muscles contain extraordinarily high concentrations of myoglobin, an oxygen-binding protein that stores oxygen directly in muscle tissue. Unlike land mammals, seals can also collapse their lungs safely under high pressure, preventing nitrogen gas from dissolving into their bloodstream and avoiding the dangerous condition known as the bends.

Today we will discuss how plants communicate and defend themselves against herbivores using volatile organic compounds. When an insect, such as a caterpillar, begins chewing on a plant's leaves, the plant does not simply remain passive. Instead, it releases specific chemical signals into the air known as volatile organic compounds. These airborne chemicals serve multiple defensive functions. First, they can act as a direct deterrent, making the leaves unpalatable to attacking pests. Second, and perhaps most remarkably, these volatile compounds act as distress signals that travel across the air to neighboring plants, warning them of impending herbivore attacks. Upon receiving these chemical warnings, neighboring plants proactively activate their own internal defense mechanisms, such as producing bitter chemical toxins before the insects even arrive. Furthermore, these scented signals can attract predatory wasps, which hunt the caterpillars, providing indirect biological defense for the plant.

o: They stimulate faster vertical growth towards sunlight.

Today we will examine the life cycle of stars and focus specifically on how white dwarfs evolve. A white dwarf represents the evolutionary endpoint of low-to-medium-mass stars, roughly similar in mass to our Sun. Once such a star exhausts the hydrogen fuel in its core, it expands into a red giant before eventually shedding its outer atmospheric layers into space, forming a glowing planetary nebula. What remains behind is an extremely dense, Earth-sized stellar core composed primarily of degenerate carbon and oxygen. Although a white dwarf contains about as much mass as our Sun packed into the volume of our planet, it possesses no internal nuclear fusion reactions to generate energy. Today we will discuss the geological mechanics of continental drift and focus on paleomagnetism as primary evidence for plate tectonics. Paleomagnetism is the study of the record of Earth's magnetic field preserved in magnetic minerals within volcanic rocks. When molten basaltic lava cools and solidifies at mid-ocean ridges, iron-bearing minerals, such as magnetite, align themselves parallel to the direction of Earth's magnetic field at that exact moment in geological time. Once the rock cools completely below its Curie point, that magnetic orientation becomes permanently locked in place. As scientists surveyed ocean floor rocks across the globe, they discovered a striking pattern of alternating magnetic stripes running parallel to oceanic ridges. These symmetrical magnetic strips record historical geomagnetic reversals, where Earth's north and south magnetic poles swapped places over millions of years. Because these magnetic anomaly patterns match perfectly on either side of ridge axes, they provided definitive proof for seafloor spreading.

Today we will examine the economic concept of supply and demand, focusing specifically on market equilibrium. In microeconomics, market equilibrium occurs precisely at the price point where the quantity of a good that producers are willing to supply matches the quantity that consumers are willing to buy. When the market price of a product is set above this equilibrium point, a surplus occurs because producers generate more goods than consumers demand, forcing sellers to lower their prices to clear their inventory. Today we will discuss the psychological phenomenon known as cognitive dissonance, originally proposed by Leon Festinger in nineteen-fifty-seven. Cognitive dissonance refers to the mental discomfort or psychological stress a person experiences when holding two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values simultaneously, or when performing actions that contradict their personal moral convictions. According to Festinger's theory, this internal conflict creates an uncomfortable state of tension that motivates individuals to seek psychological relief. People typically resolve this dissonance in one of three ways: by changing their conflicting behavior, by justifying their actions by acquiring new information, or by minimizing the importance of the conflicting belief. For example, individuals who purchase an expensive luxury car that turns out to have poor fuel efficiency might experience dissonance, which they resolve by convincing themselves that safety and comfort are far more important than fuel economy.

Today we will examine the transition from nomadic hunter-gatherer societies to settled agricultural communities during the Neolithic Revolution, approximately twelve thousand years ago. This monumental shift in human history began in the Fertile Crescent region of the Near East. Instead of continuously migrating to forage for wild plants and hunt migratory game, early human groups discovered how to domesticate wild cereal grains like wheat and barley, along with livestock such as sheep and goats. This domestication process allowed communities to produce consistent food surpluses, which in turn supported permanent settlements, population growth, and occupational specialization. Today we will explore the origins of the Baroque musical era, which flourished across Europe from approximately sixteen hundred to seventeen fifty. A defining characteristic of Baroque music is the development of polyphonic texture, where multiple independent melodic voices intertwine simultaneously to create a rich auditory tapestry. This era also witnessed the birth of opera in Italy, combining dramatic theatrical storytelling with expressive vocal solos and orchestral accompaniment. Furthermore, Baroque composers introduced the basso continuo, an instrumental accompaniment bassline that provided harmonic structure and rhythmic drive throughout musical compositions. Psychologists use the term «cognitive load» to describe the amount of mental effort needed to process information. Working memory, the system that holds and manipulates information for short periods, has a limited capacity. When a task requires too many elements to be processed at once, performance drops and learning becomes less effective.

Researchers distinguish between different sources of load. Intrinsic load comes from the complexity of the material itself; learning advanced mathematics, for instance, naturally demands more effort than learning a list of colors. Extraneous load, by contrast, is created by the way information is presented. A diagram whose labels are placed far from the parts they describe forces the learner to search back and forth, wasting limited mental resources.

The practical implication is that teachers and designers can improve learning without making content easier. In economics, a «public good» has two key features. It is non-excludable, meaning that it is difficult to prevent anyone from using it, and non-rivalrous, meaning that one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others. Street lighting is a classic example: once a street is lit, everyone walking there benefits, and one pedestrian's use of the light does not leave less for others.

These features create what economists call the «free-rider problem». Because people can enjoy a public good without paying for it, private companies often have little incentive to provide it. If a business built a lighthouse, for instance, it would find it nearly impossible to charge every passing ship. As a result, many public goods are funded by governments through taxes or by community organizations.

Not all goods fit neatly into categories. A public park may become rivalrous when it is crowded, and a television broadcast can become excludable if it requires a subscription. For this reason, some economists prefer to think of «publicness» as a matter of degree rather than a strict definition.

The Japanese art of woodblock printing, called ukiyo-e, became popular in the 17th to 19th centuries. Artists created images by carving designs into blocks of wood. Each color required a separate block, and printers carefully pressed paper onto one block after another to build up the final picture. Because many copies could be made, prints were cheap enough for ordinary city people to buy.

Ukiyo-e often showed everyday life, actors, travelers and landscapes. Hokusai's «The Great Wave off Kanagawa», printed around 1831, is probably the most famous example. In the late 19th century, Japanese prints reached Europe, where they influenced painters such as Van Gogh and Monet, who admired their bold colors and unusual compositions.

passage:
For most of history, astronomers could only study the universe using visible light. In the twentieth century, however, scientists began building telescopes that detect other forms of electromagnetic radiation, from radio waves to X-rays. Each type reveals different features. Radio telescopes, for instance, can observe cold gas clouds where new stars are forming, while X-ray telescopes detect extremely hot material near black holes.

Because Earth's atmosphere blocks much of this radiation, many of these instruments must be placed in space. Infrared light, which can pass through dust that hides visible stars, is especially valuable for studying distant galaxies. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, observes mainly in infrared and orbits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, where it is kept extremely cold so that its own heat does not interfere with its observations.

By combining data from many wavelengths, astronomers can build a far more complete picture of objects than any single telescope could provide.

Professor: Many universities now offer courses completely online. Do you think online courses are as effective as traditional classroom courses? Why or why not?

Claire: I think online courses can be just as effective. Students can watch lectures again and study at their own pace.

Andrew: I disagree. In a classroom, students can ask questions immediately and learn from discussions with classmates.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: I understand Andrew's point about immediate questions, but I agree with Claire that online courses can be equally effective, as long as they are well designed. In my experience, the biggest advantage is flexibility. Many students work part-time, and online courses let them study when they are most focused instead of sitting in a lecture after a long shift. Moreover, modern platforms are not limited to recorded videos. Discussion forums and live video sessions allow students to ask questions and work in groups. For example, in my online statistics course, we had weekly live problem-solving sessions, and I actually participated more than in face-to-face classes because I felt less nervous. Therefore, the format matters less than the quality of the course design.

Professor: Some people believe that governments should spend more money on public transportation, while others think the money should be used to improve roads. Which do you think is more important, and why?

Priya: Public transportation is more important because it reduces traffic and pollution.

Marcus: I think roads are more important. Many people live in rural areas where buses and trains are not practical.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: Marcus makes a fair point about rural areas, but I believe public transportation should be the priority in most countries. Priya mentioned traffic and pollution, and I would add another reason: equality of opportunity. Not everyone can afford a car, especially young people, students and older adults. A reliable bus or train network allows them to reach jobs, schools and hospitals. For instance, when my city opened a new tram line, people in the outer neighborhoods suddenly had access to jobs in the center within thirty minutes. Of course, roads still need maintenance, but building more roads usually just attracts more cars. Investing in public transportation helps a larger number of people in a sustainable way.
tips: Reconoce el argumento contrario («makes a fair point») y luego refútalo.
«I would add another reason» = idea nueva: es lo que más puntúa.
Mantén 120-150 palabras sin errores.

Professor: When students work on group projects, should each student receive an individual grade, or should the whole group receive the same grade? Explain your view.

Omar: Everyone should get the same grade. It encourages students to cooperate and help each other.

Hana: Individual grades are fairer, because some students do much more work than others.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: Both Omar and Hana raise valid concerns, but I think the best solution is a combination of the two approaches. A shared grade, as Omar says, motivates the team to work together. However, when the entire grade is shared, hardworking students can feel frustrated, which supports Hana's view. In my opinion, professors could give, for example, seventy percent of the grade to the group's final product and thirty percent to each student's individual contribution, measured through peer evaluations and short personal reflections. I experienced this system in a marketing course last year, and it worked well: everyone cooperated, but no one could simply rely on others. This balanced system rewards teamwork while still being fair to individuals.
tips: Una postura intermedia original también cuenta como «idea nueva».
Propón algo concreto (70 % / 30 %).
Conecta con «However», «In my opinion», «This balanced system…».

Professor: Should high schools require students to learn a second language? Why or why not?

Leo: Yes. Learning a language helps students understand other cultures.

Sara: No. Students should be free to choose subjects that match their career goals.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: I agree with Leo that high schools should require a second language, but for an additional reason: it improves thinking skills. Studying a new language trains memory and helps students notice how their own language works. I understand Sara's concern about freedom of choice, but a second language is useful in almost every career today. Companies trade internationally, and even local jobs in tourism or health care often involve speaking with people from other countries. In my case, learning English at school allowed me to read research and take online courses that are not available in my first language. For these reasons, I believe a second language should be a basic part of every student's education.
tips: Apoya a uno y añade una razón distinta a la suya.

Professor: Some cities are banning cars from their downtown areas. Do you think this is a good policy? Explain why or why not.

Elena: It's a great idea. City centers become cleaner, quieter and safer for pedestrians.

David: I'm not sure. Shops in the center might lose customers who usually come by car.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: David's concern about local shops is understandable, but I believe car-free downtowns are a good policy if they are introduced carefully. Elena focuses on the environment and safety, and I'd add that these areas can actually help businesses. When streets are pleasant to walk in, people tend to stay longer and visit more shops and cafés. Several European cities, such as Pontevedra in Spain, reported more pedestrian activity in the center after restricting traffic. To protect shops, however, the city should provide good public transportation and parking areas just outside the zone, as well as delivery hours for businesses. With these measures, a car-free center can benefit residents, visitors and shop owners alike.
tips: Convierte la objeción en tu argumento («can actually help businesses»).
Un ejemplo real da autoridad; si no lo sabes seguro, usa uno personal.

Professor: Is it better for students to take a gap year before starting university, or to begin university immediately after high school? Explain your answer.

Noah: A gap year gives students time to work, travel and decide what they really want to study.

Mei: Starting immediately is better. Students keep their study habits and finish their degree sooner.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: Mei's argument about study habits is reasonable, but I agree with Noah that a gap year can be very valuable, especially for students who are unsure about their major. Changing majors halfway through university costs time and money, so a year spent exploring interests can actually save time in the long run. In addition, working for a year teaches responsibility and budgeting, which helps students manage university life. A friend of mine worked at a veterinary clinic during her gap year and realized she wanted to study biology instead of business. However, a gap year needs a clear plan; without goals, it can easily become a year of doing nothing. With a plan, it is a smart investment.
tips: Rebate el argumento contrario usando su propio criterio (el tiempo).
«In addition» + ejemplo concreto.
Matiza al final: «However, … needs a clear plan».

Professor: Many museums now offer virtual tours online. Do you think virtual tours can replace visiting a museum in person? Why or why not?

Anna: Virtual tours are amazing. Anyone in the world can see famous collections for free.

Karim: They can't replace real visits. Seeing the actual size and texture of an object is a completely different experience.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: I agree with Karim that virtual tours cannot fully replace real visits, although Anna is right that they make collections far more accessible. In my view, the two serve different purposes. A virtual tour is excellent for preparation and research: before visiting the Alhambra, I explored it online and learned about its history, so the real visit was much more meaningful. However, the physical experience includes things a screen cannot provide, such as the scale of a building, the light, and even the sounds of the place. Museums are also social spaces where families and school groups learn together. Therefore, virtual tours should be seen as a complement that encourages people to visit, not as a replacement.
tips: Una postura de «complemento, no sustituto» suele dar ideas nuevas.
Ejemplo personal con detalle sensorial.
Concluye respondiendo directamente a la pregunta.

Professor: Should universities require all students to take a physical education class? Explain your opinion.

Tom: Yes. Many students sit all day, and exercise improves both health and concentration.

Lina: No. University students are adults and should decide for themselves.

Write at least 100 words. You have 10 minutes.
model: Lina is right that university students are adults, but I support Tom's idea, with one condition: students should be able to choose the activity. Tom mentioned health and concentration, and I would add that sports help students make friends, which is important in the first year when many feel lonely. If the requirement offers many options, such as swimming, hiking, football or yoga, students still have freedom while building a healthy habit. At my university, first-year students can choose from twenty activities, and most of my classmates continued playing their sport after the requirement ended. In conclusion, a flexible physical education requirement respects students' choices and improves their wellbeing.
tips: Combina las dos posturas con una condición.
Añade un beneficio nuevo (amistades) que nadie mencionó.
Usa «In conclusion» para cerrar.
